nodes.name: Data separability problem for neural networks
nodes.statement: Consider two bounded, possibly infinite sets $X^{+}, X^{-}\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ that are \emph{$\delta$-separated,} i.e., $\Vert x^{+}-x^{-}\Vert \geq \delta$ for all $x^{+}\in X^{+}$ and $x^{-}\in X^{-}$. Let $F: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{n}$ denote the function defined by a feedforward neural network. The fundamental problem of data separability asks if $F(X^{+})$ and $F(X^{-})$ are \emph{linearly separable}, i.e., if there exists a nonzero vector $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and constant $c$ such that \[{a^{\intercal}F(x)+c}=\begin{cases} > 0 &\textup{if }x\in X^{+}\\ < 0 &\textup{if }x\in X^{-} \end{cases},\] in which case the \emph{margin of separation} is $\inf\lbrace \vert a^{\intercal}y+c\vert/\Vert a\Vert :y\in F(X^{+}\cup X^{-})\rbrace$.
nodes.statement_short: Given two δ-separated bounded sets and a feedforward network F, are F(X+) and F(X-) linearly separable, and with what margin?

nodes.name: δ-separated sets

nodes.name: Linear separability and margin of separation
nodes.statement: The fundamental problem of data separability asks if $F(X^{+})$ and $F(X^{-})$ are \emph{linearly separable}, i.e., if there exists a nonzero vector $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and constant $c$ such that \[{a^{\intercal}F(x)+c}=\begin{cases} > 0 &\textup{if }x\in X^{+}\\ < 0 &\textup{if }x\in X^{-} \end{cases},\] in which case the \emph{margin of separation} is $\inf\lbrace \vert a^{\intercal}y+c\vert/\Vert a\Vert :y\in F(X^{+}\cup X^{-})\rbrace$.
nodes.statement_short: F(X+), F(X-) are linearly separable if some affine function a^T F(x)+c is positive on X+ and negative on X-; the margin is the minimal normalized distance.

nodes.name: Index set [n]
nodes.statement: For any $n\in \mathbb{N}$, let $[n]:=\lbrace 1, 2, \dots , n\rbrace$.

nodes.name: Euclidean norm
nodes.statement: Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ be the Euclidean norm.

nodes.name: Euclidean ball
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{B}_{2}^d(c,R) = \{x\in \mathbb{R}^d:\Vert x-c\Vert \le R\}$.

nodes.name: Ball shorthand R B_2^d
nodes.statement: We use the shorthand $R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}:=\mathbb{B}_{2}^d(0,R)$.

nodes.name: Unit sphere
nodes.statement: Let the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ be the surface of $\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$.

nodes.name: Distance from a point to a set
nodes.statement: Also, define the distance between any point $x\in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a set $S\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ as $\mathrm{dist}(x,S) :=\inf \lbrace \|x-y\|:y\in S\rbrace$.

nodes.name: Rectified linear activation function (ReLU)
nodes.statement: In this paper, our standalone choice of activation function is the \emph{rectified linear activation function} ($\relax$) defined by $\relax (x) = x\mathbf{1}_{\lbrace x\ge 0\rbrace}$ and extended to $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ coordinate-wise.

nodes.name: Standard Gaussian matrix and vector notation
nodes.statement: We denote the standard Gaussian matrix and vector where each entry is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) as $\relax(0,1)$ by $\relax(0, I_{n\times d})$ and $\relax(0, I_{d})$ with appropriate dimensions.

nodes.name: One-layer neural network
nodes.statement: For a one-layer NN, it is $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{n}$ where $\Phi (x)=\relax(Wx+b)$ for weights $W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and bias $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

nodes.name: (δ, μ)-mutual complexity
nodes.statement: We say two $\delta$-separated sets $X^{-}, X^{+}\subset R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$ have \emph{$( \delta, \mu )$-mutual complexity} $N$, if $N=N^- + N^+$ is the minimum positive integer such that there exist two finite sets of \emph{centers} $C^+ = \{c_i^+\}_{i=1}^{N^+}\subset \mathbb{R}_2^d$ and $C^- = \{c_i^-\}_{i=1}^{N^-}\subset \mathbb{R}^d$, and two sets of constants $r_1^+, r_2^+, \ldots, r_{N^+}^+, r_1^-, r_2^-, \ldots, r_{N^-}^- \ge 0$ of \emph{radii} satisfying \begin{enumerate} \item $\bigcup_{i=1}^{N^+} X^+_i$ and $c_i^+\in\mathrm{conv} (X^+_i)$ where $X^+_i := X^+\cap \mathbb{B}_2^d(c_{i}^+, r_{i}^+)$, \item $\bigcup_{j=1}^{N^-} X^-_j$ and $c_j^-\in\mathrm{conv} (X^-_j)$ where $X^-_j := X^-\cap \mathbb{B}_2^d(c_{j}^-, r_{j}^-)$, \item $r_i^+ \le \mu^{-1}\mathrm{dist}^{2}\left(c_i^+, C^{-}\right)$, \item $r_j^- \le \mu^{-1}\mathrm{dist}^{2}\left(c_j^-, C^{+}\right)$, \item and $C^{+}, C^{-}$ are $\delta$-separated \end{enumerate} for every $i\in [N^+]$ and $j\in [N^-]$. As a special case where $\mu\to \infty$, the \emph{mutual complexity} of two finite sets $X^{+}$ and $X^{-}$ is the cardinality $N=\vert X^+\vert +\vert X^-\vert$.
nodes.statement_short: N is the least number of centers C+, C- (δ-separated, in the convex hulls of their clusters) whose balls of radius ≤ μ^{-1}dist^2 to the opposite centers cover X+ and X-.
nodes.label: def:complexity

nodes.name: Separation by one-layer RINN (exponential-in-d width)
nodes.statement: Fix any $\eta \in (0, 1)$ and $\delta$-separated $X^{+}, X^{-}\subset R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$ with $d\geq 2$. \begin{itemize} \item If $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite, let $N:=\vert X^{+}\vert +\vert X^{-}\vert$, and let $\gamma: =\delta^{2}/8Rd$. \item Otherwise, let $N$ be the $(\delta, 64\delta^{-2}R^{3}d)$-mutual complexity of $X^+$ and $X^-$, and let $\gamma:= \delta^2/16Rd$. \end{itemize} For a one-layer RINN $\Phi(x):=\relax(Wx+b)$ with weights $W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and bias $b\sim \mathrm{Unif}\left([-\lambda, \lambda]^n\right)$, the sets $\Phi(X^{+}), \Phi (X^{-})\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are linearly separable with probability at least $1-\eta$ by a margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma,N)$ if width $n$ and maximal bias $\lambda$ satisfy either of the following, depending on how weights $W$ is sampled: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $n\geq \frac{\log (N/\eta)}{p}$ and $\lambda\geq R$ if each row of the weight matrix $W_i\stackrel{iid}{\sim} \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$, \item[(ii)] $n\geq \frac{10\log (N/\eta)}{p}$ and $\lambda\geq 3R\sqrt{d}$ if weights $W\sim \relax(0, I_{n\times d})$ are Gaussian, \end{enumerate} where we recall that $\relax(0, I_{n\times d})$ means each entry is i.i.d. $\relax(0, 1)$, and define \begin{equation} p:=\frac{R}{8(d-1)\lambda}\left(\frac{\delta^{2}}{8R^{2}}\right)^{d}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{M}(\gamma,N):=\sqrt{\frac{4R(R+\gamma)}{N(1+2R/\gamma)^{2N}-N}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A one-layer ReLU RINN with uniform-sphere or Gaussian weights and uniform bias makes δ-separated sets linearly separable w.p. ≥1-η once width ≳ log(N/η)/p.

nodes.name: Separation of ℓ-many δ-separated sets
nodes.statement: \cref{thm:main} can be extended to show the separation capacity of $\Phi$ for $\ell$-many $\delta$-separated sets by running the argument between each set and the union of the remaining sets. Let $N$ be the total number of points if the sets are finite, or the $(\delta, 64\delta^{-2}R^3d)$-mutual complexity of all sets otherwise. For any $\eta\in (0, 1)$, with $\ell$ times the width lower bound, $\Phi$ makes each set linearly separable from the rest with the same margin and probability at least $1-\ell\eta$ by a union bound.
nodes.statement_short: With ℓ times the width, Φ separates each of ℓ δ-separated sets from the union of the rest w.p. ≥1-ℓη, by a union bound.
assumptions: Let $N$ be the total number of points if the sets are finite, or the $(\delta, 64\delta^{-2}R^3d)$-mutual complexity of all sets otherwise.
For any $\eta\in (0, 1)$, with $\ell$ times the width lower bound
conclusions: $\Phi$ makes each set linearly separable from the rest with the same margin and probability at least $1-\ell\eta$

nodes.name: Gaussian width
nodes.statement: To state it, we define the \emph{Gaussian width} $w(T)$ of a subset $T\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ (\cite[Definition~7.5.1]{Ver18}) as \begin{equation} w(T) := \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{x\in T} g^{\intercal}x\right] \text{ where } g\sim \relax(0, I_{n}). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Gaussian width formula
nodes.statement: w(T) := \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{x\in T} g^{\intercal}x\right] \text{ where } g\sim \relax(0, I_{n}).
nodes.label: eq:w

nodes.name: Separation by one-layer Gaussian RINN (dimension-free width)
nodes.statement: There exists a constant $C = C(\delta, R)>0$ such that the following holds. Fix any $\eta \in (0, 1)$ and $\delta$-separated $X^{+}, X^{-}\subset R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$ with $d\geq 2$. \begin{itemize} \item If $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite, let $N:=\vert X^{+}\vert +\vert X^{-}\vert$, and let $\gamma: =\delta^{2}/18R\sqrt{k}$. \item Otherwise, let $N$ be the $(\delta, 144\delta^{-2}R^{3}\sqrt{k})$-mutual complexity of $X^+$ and $X^-$, and let $\gamma:= \delta^{2}/36R\sqrt{k}$, where in both cases we let \begin{equation} k := C\left(\frac{32R}{\delta^2}\right)^2\left(w\left((X^+-X^-)\cup X^+\cup X^-\right)^2+R^2\right). \end{equation} \end{itemize} For a one-layer RINN $\Phi(x):=\relax(Wx+b)$ with standard Gaussian weights $W\sim \relax(0, I_{n\times d})$ and bias $b\sim \mathrm{Unif}\left([-\lambda, \lambda]^n\right)$, the sets $\Phi(X^{+}), \Phi (X^{-})\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are linearly separable with probability at least $1-\eta$ by a margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma,N)$ defined in \eqref{eq:p}, provided maximal bias $\lambda \geq 9R\sqrt{k}/8$ and width \begin{equation} n \geq \frac{\log (N/\eta)}{q}, \quad \text{where}\quad q :=\frac{R}{4\lambda \sqrt{k}}\left(\frac{2\delta^2}{81R^2}\right)^k. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: With Gaussian weights and λ ≥ 9R√k/8, width ≥ log(N/η)/q suffices, where k depends on Gaussian widths, not on the ambient dimension d.

nodes.name: Proof strategy for the main theorems
nodes.statement: Our primary focus lies on providing a proof sketch when dealing with finite sets $X^{+}$ and $X^{-}$. Extending this proof to arbitrary sets is fairly straightforward. To maintain brevity, we will present a brief sketch of the argument for separation while omitting the margin of guarantee. Additionally, we will freely switch between the uniform unit row vector and the standard Gaussian initializations of the weight matrix $W$ in \cref{thm:main}, with a brief comment on their similarities. The following interpretation of a one-layer neural network $\Phi$ is central to our argument: recall that $i$-th node of $\Phi$ encodes the $i$-th row $W_i$ of the weight matrix $W$ and the $i$-th entry $b_i$ of $b$, i.e., $\left(\Phi(x)\right)_{i} = \relax\left(W_{i}^{\intercal}x+b_{i}\right)$. For any $x\in \mathbb{R}^n$, assuming that $W_i\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ is normalized, $h_i(x)=W^{\intercal}_ix+b_i$ is the signed distance between $x$ and the hyperplane $\lbrace h_i=0\rbrace$. Thus, $(\Phi(x))_{i}$ measures the distance of $x$ and $h_i$ if $x$ is on the positive side of $h_i$ and is zero otherwise. \paragraph{Step 1: Constructing a Deterministic Layer $\Phi$} The first step, outlined in \cref{sec:One}, is the construction of a deterministic one-layer NN that makes $X^+$ and $X^-$ linearly separable, if they are both finite. The construction is given in \cref{alg:det_onelayer}: we enumerate all points $x_i\in X^+\cup X^-$ in descending order of norm. For each $x_i$, we will find a hyperplane $h_i$ where $x_i$ is on the positive side of $h_i$ and all $x_j$ in the opposite class with $j>i$ (i.e. $\Vert x_j\Vert \le\Vert x_i\Vert$ are on the negative side of $h_i$. This condition is formalized as $B_i$ in \cref{thm:prob}. \paragraph{Step 2: Showing $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are Linearly Separable} We find the separating hyperplane via \cref{alg:weights}. This amounts to finding a vector $a$ such that $a^{\intercal}\Phi(x^{+}) >0$ for every $x^{+}\in X^{+}$ and $a^{\intercal}\Phi(x^{-}) <0$ for every $x^{-}\in X^{-}$. Using the above guarantee, we will construct $a$ coordinate-by-coordinate recursively, with $a_i$ chosen so that $a$ separates $\Phi(X^{+})$ and $\Phi (X^{-})$. \paragraph{Step 3: Passing to a Randomly Initialized Layer} Under random initialization, we need two additional ideas: first, by \cref{lem:proj}, if a layer makes the sets linearly separable, it continues to do so after adding more nodes. The second idea, shown in \cref{thm:prob}, is to argue that the event $B_i$ occurs with positive probability for a randomly chosen hyperplane $h_i$. Combining these ideas, when the width is sufficiently large, we can find for every $i$ a copy of $h_i$ satisfying $B_i$ in the random layer. These together makes $X^+$ and $X^-$ linearly separable. \paragraph{Step 4: Generalizing to Arbitrary Sets} To obtain the result for arbitrary sets, we use the notion of mutual complexity in \cref{def:complexity} which is influenced by \cite{dirksen2021separation}. Roughly, the idea is to cover the sets with disjoint balls of small radius, and run the argument on the finite sets of centers $C^+$ and $C^-$. Upon choosing parameters carefully, we will show the linear separability of $\Phi(C^+)$ and $\Phi(C^-)$ implies that of $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ , with some margins, as in \cref{thm:arb}. \paragraph{Step 5: Uniform versus Gaussian Random Weight Matrix} We briefly comment on the two choices of random initialization of our weight matrices. While our analysis seems to be tailored for weight matrix $W$ with rows being uniform random unit vectors, and we use simple results like \cref{lem:prob lm} and \cref{prop:chi} to translate into the Gaussian case, the Gaussian case is far from an afterthought. In particular, in \cref{thm:prob}(iii), we factor a Gaussian vector into a Gaussian matrix and a uniform random unit vector, as in \cite[Proof of Theorem 1.6]{dirksen2021separation}, and apply a matrix deviation inequality in \cite[Exercise 9.1.8]{Ver18} to get a bound independent of $d$, thereby escaping the curse of dimensionality.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: build a deterministic layer with one hyperplane per point in decreasing norm order, separate its image recursively, then find these hyperplanes among random nodes and cover infinite sets by centers.

nodes.name: Projection lemma for linear separability
nodes.statement: For any $S^{+}, S^{-}\subset \mathbb{R}^{k}$ and projection $\pi$ onto a subspace indexed by coordinates $\Sigma \subset \lbrace 1, \dots , k\rbrace$, if $\pi(S^{+})$ and $\pi (S^{-})$ are linearly separable with margin $\mu$, then $S^{+}$ and $S^-$ are also linearly separable with margin at least $\mu$.
assumptions: projection $\pi$ onto a subspace indexed by coordinates $\Sigma \subset \lbrace 1, \dots , k\rbrace$
$\pi(S^{+})$ and $\pi (S^{-})$ are linearly separable with margin $\mu$
conclusions: $S^{+}$ and $S^-$ are also linearly separable with margin at least $\mu$
nodes.label: lem:proj

nodes.name: Proof of the projection lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma = \lbrace \sigma_{1}, \dots , \sigma_{\ell} \rbrace$. If $\pi(S^{+})$ and $\pi (S^{-})$ are linearly separable, then there exists $a=(a_{\sigma(x_i) })_{i}\in \mathbb{R}^{\ell}$ with $\Vert a\Vert =1$ and $b\in \mathbb{R},\mu\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ such that the hyperplane defined by $s\mapsto a^\intercal s+b$ separates $\pi(S^+)$ and $\pi(S^-)$ with margin $\mu$. Define $\tilde{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ by $\tilde{a}_i = a_i\mathbf{1}\{i\in \Sigma\}$ for $i\in [k]$. nodes.name: Sketch of the proof of Theorem 2.5
nodes.statement: This proof is extremely technical. Using \cref{fig:drawing}, we first sketch the main idea for all three cases, before proceeding to prove each case in detail. For each $i$, we draw two balls $\mathbb{B}^d_2(x_i,\delta)$ and $\|x_i\|\mathbb{B}_2^d$ as in the left picture in \cref{fig:drawing}. As $x_i$ is $\delta$-separated from all $x$ such that $\sigma(x)\neq \sigma(x_i)$, the points $x_j$ with higher index than $x_i$(i.e., smaller norm) and different \emph{sign} (e.g. the blue points $x_{i+1}$ and $x_{i+2}$) must lie in $\|x_i\|\mathbb{B}_2^d\backslash \mathbb{B}^d_2(x_i,\delta)$. In particular, they lie below the orange hyperplane formed by the intersection of the surfaces of the two balls. Roughly, we see that the distance between the orange hyperplane and $x_i$ is large enough compared to the choices of $\gamma$, so we can find a hyperplane $h$ through the region between $x_i$ and the orange hyperplane while maintaining distance at least $\gamma$ to both of them. We see that any such $h$ satisfies $B_i$ as all $x_j$'s lie below the orange hyperplane, so their distance to $h$ is at least that of the orange hyperplane, namely $\gamma$. Now, we discuss how to bound probability of this occurring when $h$ is chosen randomly as in (i), (ii), and (iii). For Case (i) where $v\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$, we condition on $v$ being close to $x_i/\Vert x_i\Vert$. Then, $h$ will be roughly parallel to the orange hyperplane with normal vector $x_i$, so we can lower bound the probability that $t$ translates $h$ to go through the region while maintaining a $\gamma$ distance. Case (ii) follows by relating the Gaussian $v$ to the uniform $v$ in Case (i). We also reduce Case (iii) to Case (i). To escape the curse of dimensionality, we use a trick to convert the ambient space to $\mathbb{R}^k$ with lower dimension: by \cite[Proof of Theorem 1.6]{dirksen2021separation}, $v\sim \relax(0, I_d)$ is distributed identically as $G^{\intercal}u$ with independent $G\sim \relax(0, I_{k\times d})$ and $u\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1})$ for all $k\in\relax$. Let $A:=G/\sqrt{k}$ and $H(z):=u^{\intercal}z+t/\sqrt{k}$, so $h(z) = {H(Az)}/{\sqrt{k}}$ for all $z$. We translate the condition $B_i$ on hyperplane $h$ and points $x_i$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to a condition on to a similar condition on hyperplane $H$ and points $Ax_i$ in $\mathbb{R}^k$, upon which we follow the argument of Case (i). A Matrix Deviation Inequality in \cite[Exercise 9.1.8]{Ver18} is needed to show the relevant geometry is preserved passing to $H$ and $Ax_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: x_i lies beyond the hyperplane cut by the two balls, so a hyperplane nearly parallel to it with suitable offset satisfies B_i; Gaussian and dimension-free cases reduce to the uniform case.

Since $\Vert x_j\Vert \leq \Vert x_i\Vert\leq R$ and $\left(v-\widehat{x}_{i}ight)^{\intercal}x_{j}\leq \Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert\cdot \Vert x_{j}\Vert$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, we obtain  egin{equation} v^{\intercal}x_{j} \leq \Vert x_{i}\Vert - rac{\delta^{2}}{2\Vert x_{i}\Vert} + \Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert\cdot \Vert x_{j}\Vert \leq \Vert x_{i}\Vert - rac{\delta^{2}}{2R} + R\Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert. \end{equation} Recall that $h(z)=v^{\intercal}z+t$ and $B_i$ occurs if and only if $v^{\intercal}x_i+t\geq \gamma$ and $v^{\intercal}x_j+t\leq-\gamma$ for all $j$ where $j>i$ and $\sigma (x_j)
eq\sigma (x_i)$. This is equivalent to $t\geq \gamma-v^{\intercal}x_i$ and $t\leq -\gamma-v^{\intercal}x_j$ for all such $j$. We bound $\vert v^{\intercal}x_i\vert \leq \Vert v\Vert \cdot\Vert x_i\Vert \leq R$ and similarly $\vert v^{\intercal}x_{j}\vert \leq R$. Hence, for a fixed $v$, $B_i$ occurs if \[ t\in I:=\left[\gamma - v^{\intercal}x_i, \ -\gamma - \max_{j:j>i, \sigma(x_j)
eq\sigma(x_i)}v^{\intercal}x_jight] \subset [-R, R]\subset [-\lambda, \lambda] \] as $\lambda\geq R$. Hence, we bound $\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid v)$ below from by the length of $I$ over $2\lambda$, i.e. \[ \mathbb{P}_{t}\left(B_{i}\mid vight) \geq  rac{1}{2\lambda}\left(v^{\intercal}x_{i}-\max_{j:j>i, \sigma(x_j)
eq \sigma(x_i)}( v^{\intercal}x_{j}) -2\gammaight)\geq  rac{1}{2\lambda}\left( rac{\delta^{2}}{2 R}-2R\Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert -2\gammaight)\] where the second inequality follows from \eqref{eq:vxi} and \eqref{eq:vxj}. nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Here, $v\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$. The idea is to condition on $v$ being close to $x_i/\Vert x_i\Vert$ and find which $t$ makes $h(z)=v^{\intercal}z+t$ satisfy $B_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: condition on v near x_i/‖x_i‖

nodes.name: Ordering and separation
nodes.statement: Note, for any $x_{j} \in X^{+}\cup X^{-}$ with $j >i$ and $\sigma(x_i)\neq \sigma(x_j)$, we know $\Vert x_j\Vert \leq \Vert x_{i}\Vert$ by our ordering and $ \Vert x-x_{i}\Vert\geq \delta$ by $\delta$-separation.
nodes.statement_short: Opposite points j>i have smaller norm and distance ≥ δ

nodes.name: Inner product bound
nodes.statement: First, for any $j$ as in the definition of $B_i$, we show $x_i^{\intercal}x_j\leq \Vert x_i\Vert ^2 - \delta^2/2$ as follows: \[ \delta^{2} \le (x_{i}-x_{j})^{\intercal}(x_{i}-x_{j}) = \Vert x_{i}\Vert ^{2}+\Vert x_{j}\Vert^{2}-2x_{i}^{\intercal}x_{j} \leq 2\Vert x_i\Vert ^{2}-2x_{i}^{\intercal}x_{j}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Show x_i^T x_j ≤ ‖x_i‖^2 − δ^2/2

nodes.name: Lower bound on v^T x_i
nodes.statement: Now, define $\widehat{x}_{i}=x_{i}/\Vert x_{i}\Vert$. For every $v\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, we note $\widehat{x}_i^{\intercal}x_i=\Vert x_i\Vert\leq R$ and bound $\left(v-\widehat{x}_{i}\right)^{\intercal}x_{i}\geq-\|v-\widehat{x}_{i}\|\cdot \|x_{i}\|$ by Cauchy-Schwarz to obtain \begin{equation} v^{\intercal}x_{i} = \widehat{x}_{i}^{\intercal}x_{i} + \left(v-\widehat{x}_{i}\right)^{\intercal}x_{i} \geq \Vert x_{i}\Vert - \Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert \cdot \Vert x_{i}\Vert\geq \Vert x_{i}\Vert - R\Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz gives (2.2)

nodes.name: Upper bound on v^T x_j
nodes.statement: Now, for any $j$ as in the definition of $B_i$, write $v^{\intercal}x_{j} = \widehat{x}_{i}^{\intercal}x_{j} + \left(v-\widehat{x}_{i}\right)^{\intercal}x_{j}$. We had $x_i^{\intercal}x_j\leq \Vert x_i\Vert ^2 - \delta^2/2$, so $\widehat{x}_i^{\intercal}x_j\leq \Vert x_i\Vert - \delta^2/2\Vert x_i\Vert$. Since $\Vert x_j\Vert \leq \Vert x_i\Vert\leq R$ and $\left(v-\widehat{x}_{i}\right)^{\intercal}x_{j}\leq \Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert\cdot \Vert x_{j}\Vert$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, we obtain \begin{equation} v^{\intercal}x_{j} \leq \Vert x_{i}\Vert -\frac{\delta^{2}}{2\Vert x_{i}\Vert} + \Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert\cdot \Vert x_{j}\Vert \leq \Vert x_{i}\Vert -\frac{\delta^{2}}{2R} + R\Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz gives (2.3)

nodes.name: Admissible offsets
nodes.statement: Recall that $h(z)=v^{\intercal}z+t$ and $B_i$ occurs if and only if $v^{\intercal}x_i+t\geq \gamma$ and $v^{\intercal}x_j+t\leq-\gamma$ for all $j$ where $j>i$ and $\sigma (x_j)\neq\sigma (x_i)$. This is equivalent to $t\geq \gamma-v^{\intercal}x_i$ and $t\leq -\gamma-v^{\intercal}x_j$ for all such $j$. We bound $\vert v^{\intercal}x_i\vert \leq \Vert v\Vert \cdot\Vert x_i\Vert \leq R$ and similarly $\vert v^{\intercal}x_{j}\vert \leq R$. Hence, for a fixed $v$, $B_i$ occurs if \[ t\in I:=\left[\gamma - v^{\intercal}x_i, \ -\gamma - \max_{j:j>i, \sigma(x_j)\neq\sigma(x_i)}v^{\intercal}x_j\right] \subset [-R, R]\subset [-\lambda, \lambda] \] as $\lambda\geq R$.
nodes.statement_short: B_i holds when t lies in an interval I inside [−λ, λ]

nodes.name: Conditional probability
nodes.statement: Hence, we bound $\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid v)$ below from by the length of $I$ over $2\lambda$, i.e. \[ \mathbb{P}_{t}\left(B_{i}\mid v\right) \geq \frac{1}{2\lambda}\left(v^{\intercal}x_{i}-\max_{j:j>i, \sigma(x_j)\neq \sigma(x_i)}( v^{\intercal}x_{j}) -2\gamma\right)\geq \frac{1}{2\lambda}\left(\frac{\delta^{2}}{2 R}-2R\Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert -2\gamma\right)\] where the second inequality follows from \eqref{eq:vxi} and \eqref{eq:vxj}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound P(B_i | v) by |I|/2λ

nodes.name: Spherical cap
nodes.statement: Let $r:=\left({\delta^{2}}/{4R^{2}}\right)\left(1-{1}/{d}\right)$. Now, $r\in [0,2]$ as $\delta \leq 2R$. As $v\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$, applying \cref{lem:geo lm}(1) gives \[ \mathbb{P}(B_{i}) \geq \mathbb{P}\left(B_{i}\mid \Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert \leq r\right)\cdot \mathbb{P}_{t}\left(\Vert v-\widehat{x}_{i}\Vert \leq r\right) \geq \frac{1}{2\lambda}\left(\frac{\delta^{2}}{2R}-2Rr-2\gamma\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{r}{2}\right)^{d-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.2(1) with radius r

nodes.name: Plug in
nodes.statement: Plug in $r$ and bound $\gamma \leq \delta^{2}/8Rd$ to obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}(B_{i}) & \geq \frac{1}{4\lambda}\left[\frac{\delta^{2}}{2R}-2R\cdot \frac{\delta^{2}}{4R^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{d}\right)-2\cdot \frac{\delta^{2}}{8Rd} \right]\left[\frac{\delta^{2}}{8R^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{d}\right)\right]^{d-1} \\ & = \frac{1}{4\lambda}\left(\frac{\delta^{2}}{4Rd}\right)\left(\frac{\delta^{2}}{8R^{2}}\right)^{d-1}\left(1-\frac{1}{d}\right)^{d-1} \\ & \geq \frac{R}{8(d-1)\lambda}\left(\frac{\delta^{2}}{8R^{2}}\right)^{d} \\ & = p \end{align*} where the second inequality follows from the fact that $(1-1/d)^d$ is increasing in $d$ for $d\geq 2$, so it is at least its value $1/4$ at $d=2$. This establishes Case (i).
nodes.statement_short: Substitute r and γ to get P(B_i) ≥ p

nodes.name: Proof of Case (ii) of Theorem 2.5
nodes.statement: Here, $v\sim \relax(0, I_{d})$. By \cref{lem:prob lm}(1), we can change variables to $\rho = \Vert v\Vert$ with $\rho^2\sim \chi^2_d$ and $\widehat{v}=v/\rho\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$, which are independent. For any $1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}$, we compute \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid \rho) & = \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho \geq \gamma/\rho \ \forall \ x\in X^+ \text{ and } \widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho \leq -\gamma/\rho \ \forall \ x\in X^-\right) \\ & \geq \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho \geq \gamma \ \forall \ x\in X^+ \text{ and } \widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho \leq -\gamma \ \forall \ x\in X^-\right) \\ & \geq \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho\text{ satisfies event }B_i\right). \end{align*} Now, $\widehat{v}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ and, for a fixed $\rho$, $t/\rho \sim \mathrm{Unif}([-\lambda/\rho, \lambda/\rho]$. Since $\rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}$ and $\lambda\geq 3\sqrt{d}R$, $\lambda/\rho\geq R$. Hence, Case (i) applies to show \[ \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid \rho) \geq \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho\text{ satisfies event }B_i\right) \geq p.\] This holds for every $\rho$ where $1\leq\rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}$. By conditioning on it, we obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}(B_i) & \geq \mathbb{P}\left(B_i\mid 1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}\right)\cdot \mathbb{P}\left(1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}\right) \\ & \geq \frac{1}{10}\inf\left\lbrace \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid\rho) : {1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}}\right\rbrace \\ & \geq \frac{p}{10} \end{align*} where $ \mathbb{P}(1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d})\geq 1/10$ by \cref{prop:chi}, showing Case (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Split Gaussian v into an independent radius and uniform direction; on 1 ≤ ρ ≤ 3√d apply Case (i), and that event has probability ≥ 1/10.

nodes.name: Polar decomposition
nodes.statement: Here, $v\sim \relax(0, I_{d})$. By \cref{lem:prob lm}(1), we can change variables to $\rho = \Vert v\Vert$ with $\rho^2\sim \chi^2_d$ and $\widehat{v}=v/\rho\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$, which are independent.
nodes.statement_short: Change variables to radius and direction

nodes.name: Condition on radius
nodes.statement: For any $1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}$, we compute \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid \rho) & = \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho \geq \gamma/\rho \ \forall \ x\in X^+ \text{ and } \widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho \leq -\gamma/\rho \ \forall \ x\in X^-\right) \\ & \geq \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho \geq \gamma \ \forall \ x\in X^+ \text{ and } \widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho \leq -\gamma \ \forall \ x\in X^-\right) \\ & \geq \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho\text{ satisfies event }B_i\right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an event of Case (i) type

nodes.name: Apply Case (i)
nodes.statement: Now, $\widehat{v}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ and, for a fixed $\rho$, $t/\rho \sim \mathrm{Unif}([-\lambda/\rho, \lambda/\rho]$. Since $\rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}$ and $\lambda\geq 3\sqrt{d}R$, $\lambda/\rho\geq R$. Hence, Case (i) applies to show \[ \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid \rho) \geq \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{v}^{\intercal}x+t/\rho\text{ satisfies event }B_i\right) \geq p.\]
nodes.statement_short: λ/ρ ≥ R, so Case (i) gives ≥ p

nodes.name: Average over radius
nodes.statement: This holds for every $\rho$ where $1\leq\rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}$. By conditioning on it, we obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}(B_i) & \geq \mathbb{P}\left(B_i\mid 1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}\right)\cdot \mathbb{P}\left(1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}\right) \\ & \geq \frac{1}{10}\inf\left\lbrace \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid\rho) : {1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d}}\right\rbrace \\ & \geq \frac{p}{10} \end{align*} where $ \mathbb{P}(1\leq \rho\leq 3\sqrt{d})\geq 1/10$ by \cref{prop:chi}, showing Case (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.4 gives factor 1/10

nodes.name: Proof of Case (iii) of Theorem 2.5
nodes.statement:
Following the proof sketch, we will first choose $k$ using \cite[Exercise 9.1.8]{Ver18}, so the event $E$ where the $\delta$-separation and ordering of $x_i$ is preserved happens with nontrivial probability. Then, we translate condition $B_i$ to ambient space $\mathbb{R}^k$, and show $\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E)$ is nontrivial. If $\|x_i\|$ is large, we will do a similar analysis as Case (i) in $\mathbb{R}^k$; if $\|x_i\|$ is small, we will calculate $\mathbb{P}(B_i)$ directly and see it is much larger than when $\|x_i\|$ is large. \paragraph{Step 1: Choosing Dimension $k$} For every positive integer $k$, $v\sim elax(0, I_d)$ is distributed identically as $G^{\intercal}u$ with independent $G\sim elax(0, I_{k	imes d})$ and $u\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1})$. We can require $C$ to be such that $k$ defined in \eqref{eq:k} satisfy $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}$. To specify $k$, let $A:=G/\sqrt{k}$. By \cite[Exercise 9.1.8]{Ver18}, for any constants $	heta >0$ and $\omega\in [0,1)$, there exists $C$ in the definition of $k$ in \eqref{eq:k} such that with probability at least $\omega$, for all $x\in X^+\cup X^-\cup (X^+-X^-)$,  egin{equation} \vert \Vert Ax\Vert - \Vert x\Vert \vert \leq 	heta. \end{equation} Fix $	heta:= {\delta^2}/{32R}$ and $\omega:= 8/9$, and denote the event of the above display as $E$. We can choose $C$ in \eqref{eq:k} such that $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}$ and $\mathbb{P}(E)\geq 8/9$. Note, $C$ depends on $\omega$ and $	heta$, which depends on $R$ and $\delta$. \paragraph{Step 2: Relating to Case (i)} Let $H(z):=u^{\intercal}z+t/\sqrt{k}$. For every $1\leq j\leq N$, let $y_j:=Ax_j\in\mathbb{R}^k$ and $\sigma (y_j):=\sigma (x_j)$. Note that for all $z$, $h(z) = \sqrt{k} H(Az)$, so $B_i$ holds if and only if $H(y_i)\geq \gamma/\sqrt{k}$ and $H(y_j)\leq -\gamma/\sqrt{k}$ for all $j>i$ and $\sigma(y_i)
eq \sigma(y_j)$. Let $B_i'$ be $B_i$ conditioned on $E$. Note \[\mathbb{P}(B_i)\geq \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E)\cdot \mathbb{P}(E) \geq  rac{8}{9} \cdot \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E).\] For the rest of the proof, we lower bound $\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E)$, i.e. the probability that $H(y_i)\geq \gamma/\sqrt{k}$ and $H(y_j)\leq -\gamma/\sqrt{k}$ for all $j>i$ and $\sigma(y_i)
eq \sigma(y_j)$ given $E$. By the ordering of the points by their norms, we first notice that for all $j>i$,  egin{equation} \Vert x_i\Vert +	heta \geq \Vert y_i\Vert = \Vert Ax_i\Vert \geq \Vert x_i\Vert -	heta \geq \Vert x_j\Vert-	heta \geq \Vert Ax_j\Vert -2	heta =\Vert y_j\Vert-2	heta. \end{equation} On the other hand, since $AX^+$ and $AX^-$ are $(\delta -	heta)$-separable, so $\Vert y_i -y_j\Vert\geq \delta -	heta$ whenever $\sigma (y_i)
eq\sigma (y_j)$. These conditions are similar to the $\delta$-separation assumption and ordering of $x_i$ in Case (i). We show Case (iii) in two sub-cases Case (iiia) and Case (iiib) according to whether $\Vert x_i\Vert \geq\delta/2$ or $\|x_i\|\leq \delta/2$. \paragraph{Step 3: Case (iiia)} In this case, assume $\ell:=\Vert x_i\Vert\geq \delta/2$. We follow Case (i) applied to the $y_i$'s. On the event $E$ defined in \eqref{eq:E}, for every $y_j$ with $j>i$ and $\sigma(y_j)
eq \sigma (y_i)$, by \eqref{eq:norms} and $(\delta-	heta)$-separation \[ (\delta-	heta)^{2}\leq (y_{i}-y_{j})^{\intercal}(y_{i}-y_{j}) = \Vert y_{i}\Vert ^{2}+\Vert y_{j}\Vert^{2}-2y_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j} \leq 2(\ell +	heta) ^{2}-2y_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j} \] so we have $y_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j}\leq (\ell+	heta)^2-(\delta - 	heta)^{2}/2$. Let $\widehat{y}_{i}=y_{i}/\Vert y_{i}\Vert$. For every $u\in \mathbb{S}^{k-1}$, we bound $(u-\widehat{y}_i)^{\intercal}y_i\geq -\Vert u-\widehat{y}_i\Vert \cdot \Vert y_i\Vert $ by Cauchy-Schwarz and $\ell-	heta\leq \Vert y_i\Vert \leq \ell+	heta$ from \eqref{eq:norms} to obtain  egin{equation} u^{\intercal}y_{i} = \widehat{y}_{i}^{\intercal}y_{i} + \left(u-\widehat{y}_{i}ight)^{\intercal}y_{i} \geq \Vert y_{i}\Vert - \Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert \cdot \Vert y_{i}\Vert\geq (\ell-	heta) - (\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert \end{equation} Similarly, for any $j$ where $j>i$ and $\sigma (y_j)
eq\sigma(y_i)$, we had $y_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j}\leq (\ell+	heta)^2-(\delta - 	heta)^{2}/2$, so $\widehat{y}_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j}\leq (\ell+	heta)^2/\Vert y_i\Vert -(\delta - 	heta)^{2}/2\Vert y_i\Vert$. Combined with the bound $(u-\widehat{y}_i)^{\intercal}y_j\leq \Vert u-\widehat{y}_i\Vert \cdot \Vert y_j\Vert $ by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we obtain the former inequality in the following  egin{align} u^{\intercal}y_{j} & = \widehat{y}_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j} + \left(u-\widehat{y}_{i}ight)^{\intercal}y_{j} 
onumber \ & \leq  rac{(\ell+	heta)^2}{\Vert y_i\Vert } -  rac{(\delta-	heta)^2}{2\Vert y_i\Vert }+ \Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert\cdot \Vert y_{j}\Vert 
onumber \ & \leq  rac{(\ell+	heta)^2}{\ell-	heta} -  rac{(\delta -	heta)^2}{2(\ell+	heta)}+(\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_i\Vert \end{align} where we use $\ell-	heta\leq \Vert y_i\Vert\leq \ell+	heta $ and $\Vert y_j\Vert \leq \ell+	heta$ from \eqref{eq:norms} for the latter. Recall that $H(z)=u^{\intercal}z+t/\sqrt{k}$ and $B_i$ occurs if and only if $u^{\intercal}x_i+t/\sqrt{k}\geq \gamma/\sqrt{k}$ and $u^{\intercal}x_j+t/\sqrt{k}\leq-\gamma/\sqrt{k}$ for all $j$ where $j>i$ and $\sigma (y_j)
eq\sigma (y_i)$. This is equivalent to $t\geq \gamma-\sqrt{k}u^{\intercal}y_i$ and $t\leq -\gamma-\sqrt{k}u^{\intercal}y_j$ for all such $j$. Then, for a fixed $u$, the event $B_i$ occurs if \[ t\in I : = \left[\gamma - \sqrt{k}u^{\intercal}y_i, \ -\gamma -\sqrt{k}\max_{j:j>i, \sigma(y_j)
eq\sigma(y_i)}u^{\intercal}y_jight]. \] We bound $\vert u^{\intercal}y_i\vert \leq \Vert u\Vert \cdot\Vert y_i\Vert \leq \Vert x_i\Vert +	heta \leq R+	heta$ and similarly $\vert u^{\intercal}y_{j}\vert \leq R+	heta$. Since $	heta = \delta^2/32R\leq (2R)^2/32R= R/8$ and $\lambda\geq 9R\sqrt{k}/8$, we have \[ I\subset [-\sqrt{k}(R+	heta), \sqrt{k}(R+	heta)]\subset [-9\sqrt{k}R/8, 9\sqrt{k}R/8]\subset [-\lambda, \lambda].\] So we may now bound $\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E, u)$ from below by the length of $I$ over $2\lambda$, i.e.  egin{align*} \mathbb{P}_{t}\left(B_{i}\mid E, uight) & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{2\lambda}\left(u^{\intercal}y_{i}-\max_{j:j>i, \sigma(y_j)
eq \sigma(y_i)}( u^{\intercal}y_{j}) - rac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{2\lambda}\left((\ell-	heta) - rac{(\ell+	heta)^2}{\ell-	heta} +  rac{(\delta -	heta)^2}{2(\ell+	heta)} - 2 (\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & =  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{(\delta -	heta)^2}{4(\ell+	heta)} - rac{2\ell	heta}{\ell-	heta} - (\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & =  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{(\delta -	heta)^2}{4(\ell+	heta)} - rac{2 (\delta^2/32R)}{1-	heta/\ell} - (\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \end{align*} where we plug in \eqref{eq:uyi} and \eqref{eq:uyj} for the second inequality and the last equality is due to $	heta = \delta^2/32R$. We know $\delta /2 \leq \ell \leq R$, so we have $	heta \leq \delta/16 $. Note that the expression inside the parenthesis of the last line of the above display decreases when we replace every $	heta$ by its upper bound $\delta/16$, replace $\ell$ in the first and third terms by its upper bound $R$, and replace $\ell$ in the second term by its lower bound $\delta/2$. By these substitutions, we obtain the following inequality  egin{align*} \mathbb{P}(B_{i}\mid E, u) & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{(15\delta/16)^2}{4(R+\delta/16)} - rac{2 (\delta^2/32R)}{1-(\delta/16)/(\delta/2)} - (R+\delta/16)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{(15\delta/16)^2}{4(R+R/8)} - rac{2(\delta^2/32R)}{1-(\delta/16)/(\delta/2)} - (R+R/8)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & =  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{111}{896}\cdot rac{\delta^2}{R} - (9R/8)\cdot\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{\delta^2}{18R} - (9R/8)\cdot\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vertight) \end{align*} where the second inequality follows by replacing $\delta$ by its upper bound $2R$, and the last inequality follows $\gamma \leq \delta^2\sqrt{k}/18R$ by bounding $111/896\geq 1/9$. Now, we get \[ \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E) \geq \mathbb{P}\left(t\geq \gamma -\sqrt{k}u^{\intercal}y_i\mid E, u^{\intercal}y_i\geq 0ight)\cdot \mathbb{P}( u^{\intercal}y_i\geq 0) \geq  rac{1}{2} \cdot \mathbb{P}\left(t\geq \gamma\mid Eight) \] Since the event $E$ is independent of the random variable $t$, $\mathbb{P}\left(t\geq \gamma\mid Eight) =\mathbb{P}\left(t\geq \gammaight)$. Since $t\sim\mathrm{Unif}([-\lambda, \lambda])$, $\lambda\geq 9R\sqrt{k}/8$, and $\gamma \leq \delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}$, we obtain the first inequality below \[ \mathbb{P}(t\geq \gamma)=  rac{\lambda-\gamma}{2\lambda}\geq  rac{1}{2}- rac{\delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}}{2(9R\sqrt{k})/8}= rac{1}{2}- rac{2\delta^2}{81kR^2}\geq  rac{1}{2}- rac{2(2R)^2}{162R^2}>  rac{1}{3}\] where the second inequality follows from $k\geq 2$ and $\delta \leq 2R$. nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: Following the proof sketch, we will first choose $k$ using \cite[Exercise 9.1.8]{Ver18}, so the event $E$ where the $\delta$-separation and ordering of $x_i$ is preserved happens with nontrivial probability. Then, we translate condition $B_i$ to ambient space $\mathbb{R}^k$, and show $\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E)$ is nontrivial. If $\|x_i\|$ is large, we will do a similar analysis as Case (i) in $\mathbb{R}^k$; if $\|x_i\|$ is small, we will calculate $\mathbb{P}(B_i)$ directly and see it is much larger than when $\|x_i\|$ is large.
nodes.statement_short: Choose k, translate B_i to R^k, split on ‖x_i‖

nodes.name: Step 1: choosing k
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Step 1: Choosing Dimension $k$} For every positive integer $k$, $v\sim \relax(0, I_d)$ is distributed identically as $G^{\intercal}u$ with independent $G\sim \relax(0, I_{k\times d})$ and $u\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1})$. We can require $C$ to be such that $k$ defined in \eqref{eq:k} satisfy $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}$. To specify $k$, let $A:=G/\sqrt{k}$. By \cite[Exercise 9.1.8]{Ver18}, for any constants $\theta >0$ and $\omega\in [0,1)$, there exists $C$ in the definition of $k$ in \eqref{eq:k} such that with probability at least $\omega$, for all $x\in X^+\cup X^-\cup (X^+-X^-)$, \begin{equation} \vert \Vert Ax\Vert - \Vert x\Vert \vert \leq \theta. \end{equation} Fix $\theta:= {\delta^2}/{32R}$ and $\omega:= 8/9$, and denote the event of the above display as $E$. We can choose $C$ in \eqref{eq:k} such that $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}$ and $\mathbb{P}(E)\geq 8/9$. Note, $C$ depends on $\omega$ and $\theta$, which depends on $R$ and $\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose k so the matrix deviation event E has probability ≥ 8/9

nodes.name: Gaussian factorization

nodes.statement_short: v has the law of G^T u

nodes.name: Matrix deviation event

nodes.name: Step 2: relating to Case (i)
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Step 2: Relating to Case (i)} Let $H(z):=u^{\intercal}z+t/\sqrt{k}$. For every $1\leq j\leq N$, let $y_j:=Ax_j\in\mathbb{R}^k$ and $\sigma (y_j):=\sigma (x_j)$. eq \sigma(y_j)$. Let $B_i'$ be $B_i$ conditioned on $E$. Note \[\mathbb{P}(B_i)\geq \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E)\cdot \mathbb{P}(E) \geq  rac{8}{9} \cdot \mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E).\] For the rest of the proof, we lower bound $\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E)$, i.e. the probability that $H(y_i)\geq \gamma/\sqrt{k}$ and $H(y_j)\leq -\gamma/\sqrt{k}$ for all $j>i$ and $\sigma(y_i)
eq \sigma(y_j)$ given $E$. By the ordering of the points by their norms, we first notice that for all $j>i$,  egin{equation} \Vert x_i\Vert +	heta \geq \Vert y_i\Vert = \Vert Ax_i\Vert \geq \Vert x_i\Vert -	heta \geq \Vert x_j\Vert-	heta \geq \Vert Ax_j\Vert -2	heta =\Vert y_j\Vert-2	heta. \end{equation} On the other hand, since $AX^+$ and $AX^-$ are $(\delta -	heta)$-separable, so $\Vert y_i -y_j\Vert\geq \delta -	heta$ whenever $\sigma (y_i)
eq\sigma (y_j)$. These conditions are similar to the $\delta$-separation assumption and ordering of $x_i$ in Case (i). We show Case (iii) in two sub-cases Case (iiia) and Case (iiib) according to whether $\Vert x_i\Vert \geq\delta/2$ or $\|x_i\|\leq \delta/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate B_i to R^k and record norm ordering and separation

nodes.name: Translate B_i
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Step 2: Relating to Case (i)} Let $H(z):=u^{\intercal}z+t/\sqrt{k}$. For every $1\leq j\leq N$, let $y_j:=Ax_j\in\mathbb{R}^k$ and $\sigma (y_j):=\sigma (x_j)$. nodes.name: Norm ordering
nodes.statement: For the rest of the proof, we lower bound $\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid E)$, i.e. the probability that $H(y_i)\geq \gamma/\sqrt{k}$ and $H(y_j)\leq -\gamma/\sqrt{k}$ for all $j>i$ and $\sigma(y_i)\neq \sigma(y_j)$ given $E$. nodes.statement_short: Approximate ordering (2.5) of the projected points

nodes.name: Projected separation and case split
nodes.statement: On the other hand, since $AX^+$ and $AX^-$ are $(\delta -\theta)$-separable, so $\Vert y_i -y_j\Vert\geq \delta -\theta$ whenever $\sigma (y_i)\neq\sigma (y_j)$. nodes.statement_short: Projected sets are (δ−θ)-separated; split on ‖x_i‖

nodes.name: Step 3: Case (iiia)

onumber \ & \leq  rac{(\ell+	heta)^2}{\Vert y_i\Vert } -  rac{(\delta-	heta)^2}{2\Vert y_i\Vert }+ \Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert\cdot \Vert y_{j}\Vert 
onumber \ & \leq  rac{(\ell+	heta)^2}{\ell-	heta} -  rac{(\delta -	heta)^2}{2(\ell+	heta)}+(\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_i\Vert \end{align} where we use $\ell-	heta\leq \Vert y_i\Vert\leq \ell+	heta $ and $\Vert y_j\Vert \leq \ell+	heta$ from \eqref{eq:norms} for the latter. eq\sigma (y_i)$. This is equivalent to $t\geq \gamma-\sqrt{k}u^{\intercal}y_i$ and $t\leq -\gamma-\sqrt{k}u^{\intercal}y_j$ for all such $j$. Then, for a fixed $u$, the event $B_i$ occurs if \[ t\in I : = \left[\gamma - \sqrt{k}u^{\intercal}y_i, \ -\gamma -\sqrt{k}\max_{j:j>i, \sigma(y_j)
eq\sigma(y_i)}u^{\intercal}y_jight]. \] We bound $\vert u^{\intercal}y_i\vert \leq \Vert u\Vert \cdot\Vert y_i\Vert \leq \Vert x_i\Vert +	heta \leq R+	heta$ and similarly $\vert u^{\intercal}y_{j}\vert \leq R+	heta$. eq \sigma(y_i)}( u^{\intercal}y_{j}) - rac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{2\lambda}\left((\ell-	heta) - rac{(\ell+	heta)^2}{\ell-	heta} +  rac{(\delta -	heta)^2}{2(\ell+	heta)} - 2 (\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & =  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{(\delta -	heta)^2}{4(\ell+	heta)} - rac{2\ell	heta}{\ell-	heta} - (\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & =  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{(\delta -	heta)^2}{4(\ell+	heta)} - rac{2 (\delta^2/32R)}{1-	heta/\ell} - (\ell+	heta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \end{align*} where we plug in \eqref{eq:uyi} and \eqref{eq:uyj} for the second inequality and the last equality is due to $	heta = \delta^2/32R$. We know $\delta /2 \leq \ell \leq R$, so we have $	heta \leq \delta/16 $. Note that the expression inside the parenthesis of the last line of the above display decreases when we replace every $	heta$ by its upper bound $\delta/16$, replace $\ell$ in the first and third terms by its upper bound $R$, and replace $\ell$ in the second term by its lower bound $\delta/2$. By these substitutions, we obtain the following inequality  egin{align*} \mathbb{P}(B_{i}\mid E, u) & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{(15\delta/16)^2}{4(R+\delta/16)} - rac{2 (\delta^2/32R)}{1-(\delta/16)/(\delta/2)} - (R+\delta/16)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{(15\delta/16)^2}{4(R+R/8)} - rac{2(\delta^2/32R)}{1-(\delta/16)/(\delta/2)} - (R+R/8)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & =  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{111}{896}\cdot rac{\delta^2}{R} - (9R/8)\cdot\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert -  rac{\gamma}{\sqrt{k}}ight) \ & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{\delta^2}{18R} - (9R/8)\cdot\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vertight) \end{align*} where the second inequality follows by replacing $\delta$ by its upper bound $2R$, and the last inequality follows $\gamma \leq \delta^2\sqrt{k}/18R$ by bounding $111/896\geq 1/9$. As $u\sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1})$, \cref{lem:geo lm}(1) implies the second inequality below, i.e.  egin{align*} \mathbb{P}(B_{i}\mid E) & \geq\mathbb{P}\left(B_{i}\mid E, \Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert \leq right)\cdot \mathbb{P}_{t}\left(\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert \leq right) \ & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{\delta^2}{18R} -  rac{9Rr}{8}ight) \cdot \left( rac{1}{2}ight)\left( rac{r}{2}ight)^{k-1} \ & =  rac{\sqrt{k}}{\lambda}\left( rac{\delta^2}{18R} -  rac{9R}{8}\cdot  rac{4\delta^2}{81R^2}\left(1- rac{1}{k}ight)ight) \left( rac{1}{2}ight)\left( rac{2\delta^2}{81R^2}\left(1- rac{1}{k}ight)ight)^{k-1} \ & =  rac{\sqrt{k}}{2\lambda}\left( rac{\delta^2}{18Rk}ight) \left( rac{2\delta^2}{81R^2}ight)^{k-1}\left(1- rac{1}{k}ight)^{k-1} \ & \geq  rac{\sqrt{k}}{2\lambda}\left( rac{9R}{4k}ight) \left( rac{2\delta^2}{81R^2}ight)^{k}\left(1- rac{1}{k}ight)^{-1}\left( rac{1}{4}ight) \ & \geq  rac{9}{32}\left( rac{R}{\lambda\sqrt{k}}ight) \left( rac{2\delta^2}{81R^2}ight)^{k} \end{align*} where the third inequality follows from the fact that $(1-1/k)^k$ is increasing in $k$ for $k\geq 2$, so it can be lower bounded by its value $1/4$ at $k=2$, and the last inequality is due to $(1-1/k)^{-1}\geq 1$. nodes.statement_short: Large ‖x_i‖: repeat the Case (i) argument in R^k

nodes.name: Lower bound on u^T y_i
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Step 3: Case (iiia)} In this case, assume $\ell:=\Vert x_i\Vert\geq \delta/2$. We follow Case (i) applied to the $y_i$'s. On the event $E$ defined in \eqref{eq:E}, for every $y_j$ with $j>i$ and $\sigma(y_j)\neq \sigma (y_i)$, by \eqref{eq:norms} and $(\delta-\theta)$-separation \[ (\delta-\theta)^{2}\leq (y_{i}-y_{j})^{\intercal}(y_{i}-y_{j}) = \Vert y_{i}\Vert ^{2}+\Vert y_{j}\Vert^{2}-2y_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j} \leq 2(\ell +\theta) ^{2}-2y_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j} \] so we have $y_{i}^{\intercal}y_{j}\leq (\ell+\theta)^2-(\delta - \theta)^{2}/2$. Let $\widehat{y}_{i}=y_{i}/\Vert y_{i}\Vert$. For every $u\in \mathbb{S}^{k-1}$, we bound $(u-\widehat{y}_i)^{\intercal}y_i\geq -\Vert u-\widehat{y}_i\Vert \cdot \Vert y_i\Vert $ by Cauchy-Schwarz and $\ell-\theta\leq \Vert y_i\Vert \leq \ell+\theta$ from \eqref{eq:norms} to obtain \begin{equation} u^{\intercal}y_{i} = \widehat{y}_{i}^{\intercal}y_{i} + \left(u-\widehat{y}_{i}\right)^{\intercal}y_{i} \geq \Vert y_{i}\Vert - \Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert \cdot \Vert y_{i}\Vert\geq (\ell-\theta) - (\ell+\theta)\Vert u-\widehat{y}_{i}\Vert \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Inner product bound and (2.6)

nodes.name: Upper bound on u^T y_j
nodes.statement:

eq \sigma(x_i) $}\ \geq \gamma & 	extup{if $j=i$}\ \geq 0 & 	extup{otherwise} \end{cases}. \end{equation} As in \cref{alg:weights}, we choose the weight vector $a\in\mathbb{R}^N$ by picking $a_{i}$ recursively for $i=N, N-1, \dots , 1$ as follows:  egin{equation} a_{i}= rac{\sigma(x_i)}{\gamma }\left(1+\left\vert\sum_{j=i+1}^{N}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}ight\vertight). \end{equation} Note that $a_i$ has same sign as $\sigma(x_i)$. Let $H(z) = a^{\intercal}z$ be an affine function associated with the hyperplane $\{z : H(z) = 0\}$. We first claim and prove that $H$ separates the points of $\Phi(X^{+})$ and $\Phi(X^{-})$, and then derive the lower bound on the margin of separation.  egin{claim} $H$ separates $\Phi(X^{+})$ and $\Phi(X^{-})$ with margin at least $1/\Vert a\Vert$. \end{claim}  egin{proof}[Proof of \cref{claim:H sep}] It suffices to show $H (\Phi(x_{i}))\geq 1$ if $x_{i}\in X^{+}$ and $H (\Phi(x_{i}))\leq -1$ if $x_{i}\in X^{-}$. onumber \ & = \sigma(x_i) \sum_{j<i, \sigma(x_j) =\sigma(x_i) }a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} + \sigma(x_i) \sum_{j<i, \sigma(x_j)

We consider each quantity. For each term in the first quantity, $a_j$ has the same sign as $\sigma(x_j)=\sigma(x_i)$, so  egin{equation} \sigma(x_i) \sum_{j<i, \sigma(x_j) =\sigma(x_i) }a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} = \sum_{j<i, \sigma(x_j) =\sigma(x_i) }\sigma(x_j)a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} \ge 0. \end{equation} For each term in the first quantity, $(\Phi(x_i))_j = 0$ if $j<i$ and $\sigma(x_j)

eq \sigma(x_i) }a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} = 0. \end{equation} For the third quantity, from \eqref{eq:phij} we have $(\Phi(x_{i}))_{i} \ge \gamma$, and from \eqref{eq:weight_vec_choice}, so  egin{equation} \sigma(x_i) a_{i}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{i} \ge  rac{\sigma(x_i) ^{2}}{\gamma}\left(1+\left|\sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}ight|ight)\gamma = 1+\left|\sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}ight|. \end{equation} Plugging \eqref{eq:first_term}, \eqref{eq:second_term}, and \eqref{eq:third_term} into \eqref{eq:4terms} gives the first inequality below \[ \sigma(x_i) H(\Phi(x_{i})) \geq 0 + 0 + 1+\left|\sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}ight| + \sigma(x_i) \sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} \geq 1, \] and the second inequality follows by the triangle inequality. eq \sigma(x_j)$. We start by showing for all $i$, $h_{i}(x)=0$ for some $x\in R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$. nodes.statement: We now further lower bound the margin of separation $1/\Vert a\Vert$. \begin{claim} For $a$ defined in \eqref{eq:weight_vec_choice} and $\mathcal{M}$ defined in \eqref{eq:p}, $1/\Vert a\Vert \geq \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$. \end{claim} \begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{claim:margin bd}] We first show that $(\Phi(x_i))_{j}\leq 2R$ for all $j>i$ such that $\sigma(x_i)\neq \sigma(x_j)$. We start by showing for all $i$, $h_{i}(x)=0$ for some $x\in R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$. This just follows from the observations that each of our hyperplanes $\lbrace h_i=0\rbrace$ intersects $R\mathbb{B}_2^d$ by assumption. More rigorously, consider the two cases on line 5 of \cref{alg:det_onelayer}, either way we have $h_{i}(x_{i})>0$ and $h_{i}(x_{j})\leq 0$ for some $x_{i}, x_{j}\in R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$. Then, by the intermediate value theorem, there is some $x$ on the segment $x_{i}x_{j}$ such that $h_{i}(x)=0$. Since $R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$ is convex, $x\in R\mathbb{B}^{d}_{2}$. Then, for every $y\in R\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}$, since $w_{i}\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ we have \begin{equation} \vert h_{i}(y)\vert \leq \vert h_{i}(x)\vert + \vert h_{i}(y)-h_{i}(x)\vert \leq \vert w_{i}^{\intercal}(y-x)\vert \leq \Vert w_{i}\Vert \cdot \Vert y-x\Vert \le 2R. \end{equation} Here, we used the triangle inequality to obtain the first inequality, used that $h_i(x) = 0$ to get the second inequality, applied the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality in the third inequality, and used the fact that $x,y \in R\mathbb{B}_2^d$ to get the final inequality. By using the upper bound in \eqref{eq:hiy}, \[ \vert a_{i}\vert = \frac{1}{\gamma }\left( 1+\left|\sum_{j=i+1}^{N}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}\right|\right) \leq \frac{1}{\gamma} \left(1+2R \sum_{j=i+1}^{N}\vert a_{j}\vert\right), \] where we used the triangle inequality to obtain the last inequality. We choose the weight vector $a\in\mathbb{R}^N$ by picking $a_{i}$ recursively for $i=N, N-1, \dots , 1$ as follows: \[ a_{i}=\frac{2\sigma(c_i) }{\gamma }\sup_{x\in X_i}\left(1+\left|\sum_{j=i+1}^{N}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}\right|\right)\] and so for hyperplane o$H(z)=a^{\intercal}z$, every $x_i\in X_i$, and every $i\in [N]$, \begin{align*} \sigma(x_i) H(\Phi(x_{i})) & = \sigma(x_i) \sum_{j=1}^{N}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} \\ & = \sigma(x_i) \sum_{j<i, \sigma(x_j) =\sigma(x_i) }a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} + \sigma(x_i) \sum_{j<i, \sigma(x_j) \neq \sigma(x_i) }a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} \\ & \qquad + \sigma(x_i) a_{i}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{i} + \sigma(x_i) \sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} \end{align*} by breaking into four cases similar to the proof of \cref{thm:fin}. The first term is non-negative since $a_j$ has the same sign as $\sigma(x_j)=\sigma(x_i)$ and coordinates of $\Phi(x_i)$ are non-negative due to $\relax$-activation. The second term is zero since $(\Phi(x_i))_j=0$ for such $j$ by \eqref{eq:phi}. Hence \begin{align*} \sigma(x_i) H(\Phi(x_{i})) & \geq 0 + 0 + \frac{2\sigma(x_i) ^{2}}{\gamma}\sup_{x\in X_i}\left(1+\left|\sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}\right|\right)\left(\frac{\gamma}{2}\right)+\sigma(x_i) \sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} \\ & = \sup_{x\in X_i}\left( 1+\left|\sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}\right|\right)+\sigma(x_i) \sum_{j>i}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j} \\ & \geq 1 \end{align*} by the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Recursive bound on |a_i|
nodes.statement: Thus, $H (\Phi(x_{i}))\geq 1$ if $x_{i}\in X^{+}$ and $H (\Phi(x_{i}))\leq -1$ if $x_{i}\in X^{-}$, so $H(z)=a^{\intercal}z$ separates $\Phi (X^{+})$ and $\Phi (X^{-})$. The margin of separation is at least $1/\Vert a\Vert$. We bound this as follows. Exactly as \eqref{eq:hiy}, $\vert h_{i}(y)\vert \leq 2R$ for every $y\in R\mathbb{B}_2^d$. Now, we bound each weight $a_{i}$ \[ \vert a_{i}\vert = \frac{2}{\gamma }\sup_{x\in X_i}\left( 1+\left|\sum_{j=i+1}^{N}a_{j}(\Phi(x_{i}))_{j}\right|\right) \leq \frac{2}{\gamma} \left(1+2R \sum_{j=i+1}^{N}\vert a_{j}\vert\right). \]

nodes.name: Margin bound
nodes.statement: Thus, $\vert a_{i}\vert \leq \tilde{a}_{i}$ where $\tilde{a}_{i}$ is defined recursively by $\tilde{a}_{N}= 2/\gamma = \vert a_{N}\vert$ and \[ \tilde{a}_{i} = \frac{2}{\gamma}\left(1 + 2R \sum_{j=i+1}^N \tilde{a}_j\right). \] We compute $\tilde{a}_{i}$ explicitly. Taking the successive differences \[ \tilde{a}_{i-1}-\tilde{a}_{i} = \frac{2}{\gamma}\left(1 + 2R \sum_{j=i}^N \tilde{a}_j\right) - \frac{2}{\gamma}\left(1 + 2R \sum_{j=i+1}^N \tilde{a}_j\right) = \left(\frac{4R}{\gamma}\right)\tilde{a}_{i}, \] and using the fact that $\tilde{a}_{N}= 2/\gamma$, we get \[ \tilde{a}_{i} = \frac{2}{\gamma}\left(1+\frac{4R}{\gamma}\right)^{N-i}. \] Hence, \[ \Vert a\Vert ^{2} \leq \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{4}{\gamma^{2}}\left(1+\frac{4R}{\gamma}\right)^{2(N-i)} = \frac{4}{\gamma^{2}} \cdot \frac{(1+4R/\gamma)^{2N}-1}{(1+4R/\gamma )^{2}-1} = \frac{(1+2R/(\gamma/2))^{2N}-1}{4R(R+\gamma/2)}. \] Rearranging gives desired bound on the margin: $1/\Vert a\Vert\ge \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$.

nodes.name: Sketch of the proof of the main theorems
nodes.statement: To generalize \cref{thm:fin} to one-layer RINN $\Phi$, we show that given sufficient width, for every $i$, with high probability there is a node in $\Phi$ that defines a hyperplane satisfying the conditions for $h_{i}$ in \cref{alg:det_onelayer}. Then, those nodes collected over all $i$ will make $X^{+}$ and $X^{-}$ separable, which will be enough for $\Phi$ to also make them separable. This amounts to the following two conditions: \begin{enumerate} \item The condition for each $h_{i}$ is satisfied by a random hyperplane with non-trivial probability, as shown in \cref{thm:prob}. \item The other hyperplanes that do not fulfill the conditions for any $h_{i}$ do not hurt separation, as shown in \cref{lem:proj}. \end{enumerate} Combining these ideas, we are able to prove our main results (\cref{thm:main,thm:main in k}). Again, let us sketch the main ideas (of the finite $X^-$ and $X^+$ only), and hightlight a key obstacle, before the rigorous proofs in \cref{sec:1.3}. For every $i\in [N]$ and $\ell\in [n]$, let $B_i^\ell$ be the event that the $\ell$-th random hyperplane $H_\ell$ of $\Phi$ satisfies the condition for $h_i$ on line 5 of \cref{alg:det_onelayer}. We claim that $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are separable if, for every $i$, $B_i^\ell$ holds for some $\ell$, i.e. $(\forall i)(\exists \ell)B_{i}^{\ell})$. If so, we can pick some hyperplanes in $\Phi$ to form an output of \cref{alg:det_onelayer} on $X^+, X^-$, and $\gamma$. We proceed as \cref{thm:fin} to show these hyperplanes make $X^+$ and $X^-$ separable via \cref{alg:weights}. However, it is possible that the same $H_\ell$ may satisfy the conditions of multiple $h_i$'s, so we slightly modify \cref{alg:weights} to fix this issue. This modification shrinks the separation margin by a factor of $\sqrt{N}$ compared to \cref{thm:fin,thm:arb}. Then, by \cref{lem:proj}, $\Phi$ makes $X^+$ and $X^-$ separable with the desired margin, thus proving the claim. Using \cref{thm:prob}, we see that, for every $i$ and $\ell$, $\mathbb{P} (B_{i}^{\ell})\geq p$ or $p/10$ or $q$ depending on the distribution of $\Phi$. Applying indepedence over $\ell$ and union bound over $i$, we do a standard computation to bound $\mathbb{P}((\forall i)(\exists \ell)B_{i}^{\ell})$, thereby showing the finite set cases for \cref{thm:main,thm:main in k}. For arbitrary sets $X^+$ and $X^-$, we modify apply the argument above to the centers $C^{+}$ and $C^{-}$ as guaranteed by \cref{def:complexity} to show $\Phi(C^{+})$ and $\Phi(C^{-})$ are separable. The result for $\Phi(X^{+})$ and $\Phi(X^{-})$ will then follow \cref{thm:arb}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorems 1.3 and 1.4
nodes.statement: We modify the notation slightly for convenience of proving both finite set cases and arbitrary set cases together. Fix $\gamma$ to be either $\delta^2/8Rd$ or $\delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}$ depending on the distribution of $\Phi$, as in the finite set cases. For the arbitrary set cases, the parameter will be $\gamma/2$. We show in all three cases that provided the respective width bounds are met, with probability $1-\eta$, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are linearly separable. If $\vert X^+\vert +\vert X^-\vert = N <\infty$, then $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ will be linearly separable with margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$. Otherwise, in the case of arbitrary sets, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ will be linearly separable with margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$ where $N$ is now the $(\delta, 8R^2/\gamma)$-mutual complexity. We can check it is so for $\gamma\in\lbrace \delta^2/8Rd, \delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}\rbrace$. For finite sets $X^+$ and $X^-$, recall $x_i$ and $\sigma$ from \cref{alg:det_onelayer} and \eqref{eq:sigma}. For arbitrary sets $X^+$ and $X^-$, let $C^{+}$ and $C^{-}$ be the finite sets of centers guaranteed by \cref{def:complexity} for $(\delta, 8R^2/\gamma)$-mutual complexity. Let $c_{i}$ be the point in $C^{+}\cup C^{-}$ with the $i$-th largest norm and let $\sigma : C^{+}\cup C^{-}\to \lbrace -1, +1\rbrace$ such that $\sigma (c)=+1$ if $c\in C^{+}$ and $\sigma (c)=-1$ if $c\in C^{-}$. For a random layer $\Phi(x)=\relax (Wx+b)$ with width $n$, we let $B_i^j$ for $1\leq i\leq N$ and $1\leq \ell\leq n$ be the event that the $\ell$-th random hyperplane $H_\ell(z)=W_\ell^{\intercal}z+b_\ell$ of $\Phi$ satisfies the condition for $h_i$ in \cref{alg:det_onelayer} applied to $X^+$ and $X^-$ when they are finite or on $C^+$ and $C^-$ otherwise, and parameter $\gamma$. More precisely, if $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite sets, let \begin{equation} B^{\ell}_{i}(X):=\begin{cases} \left\lbrace H_{\ell}(x_{i})\geq \gamma \right\rbrace\cap \bigcap_{j:j>i, \sigma(x_i) \neq\sigma(x_j) }\left\lbrace H_{\ell}(x_{j})\leq -\gamma \right\rbrace & \textup{if such $j$ exists} \\ \left\lbrace H_{\ell}(x_{i})\geq \gamma \right\rbrace \cap \lbrace\exists \ x\in R\mathbb{B}_2^d: H_\ell(x)\leq 0\rbrace &\textup{otherwise} \end{cases}. \end{equation} For arbitrary sets $X^+$ and $X^-$, analogously define \begin{equation} B^{\ell}_{i}(C):=\begin{cases} \left\lbrace H_{\ell}(c_{i})\geq \gamma \right\rbrace\cap \bigcap_{j:j>i, \sigma(c_i) \neq\sigma(c_j) }\left\lbrace H_{\ell}(c_{j})\leq -\gamma \right\rbrace & \textup{if such $j$ exists} \\ \left\lbrace H_{\ell}(c_{i})\geq \gamma \right\rbrace \cap \lbrace\exists \ c\in R\mathbb{B}_2^d: H_\ell(c)\leq 0\rbrace &\textup{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{equation} with $\gamma$ chosen to be either $\delta^2/8Rd$ or $\delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}$ depending on the distribution of $\Phi$. This is similar to $B_i$ in \cref{thm:prob}, except we add the case where $j$ does not exist on line 5 of \cref{alg:det_onelayer}. We now resolve the duplication issue mentioned in the proof sketch. \begin{claim} Fix $\gamma$ to be $\delta^2/8Rd$ or $\delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}$. Recall $\mathcal{M}$ from \eqref{eq:p}. Then \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose that $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite and that for every $i$, $B_i^\ell(X)$ with parameter $\gamma$ holds for some $\ell$. Then, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$. \item For arbitrary sets $X^+$ and $X^-$, suppose that for every $i$, $B_i^\ell(C)$ with parameter $\gamma$ holds for some $\ell$. Then, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin $\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$. \end{enumerate} \end{claim} \begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{claim:bilx}] We break this proof down into four steps which we outline here. First, we set up some notation to clarify why we cannot directly apply \cref{alg:weights}. Then, we use \cref{thm:fin,thm:arb} to show that if we allow a single random hyperplane $H_\ell(z)$ to satisfy the condition for two hyperplanes $h_{i_1}$ and $h_{i_2}$, it makes the sets separable. Next, we show how to remove one of such hyperplanes while still making the sets separable. Finally, we use \cref{lem:proj} to show $\Phi$ also makes the sets separable. The margin will be tracked throughout. \paragraph{Step 1: Setup} By assumption, we can define indices map $f:[N]\to [n]$ by letting $f(i)=\ell$ if $B_i^\ell$ holds, where $B_i^\ell$ is either $B_i^\ell (X)$ or $B_i^\ell (C)$ depending on whether $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite. For a given $i$, if there are multiple $\ell$ such that $B_i^\ell$ holds, define $f(i)$ to be any such $\ell$. Define the range $\Sigma :=f([N])\subset [n]$ and let $\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^N$ be the projection onto the coordinates indexed by $\Sigma$. When $f$ is not injective, we cannot apply \cref{thm:fin} directly to $\lbrace H_j:j\in\Sigma\rbrace$ since there are less than $N$ hyperplanes. Let $h_i:=H_{f(i)}$ with another \emph{duplicated} hyperplane $h_{i'}$, i.e. $h_i$ and $h_{i'}$ are two copies of $H_j$ if $f(i)=f(i')=j$. Then, $h_i$ satisfies the condition on line 5 of \cref{alg:det_onelayer} for this $i$. Consider the one-layer neural network $\Psi(x)=\relax(h_1(x), \dots, h_N(x))$. \paragraph{Step 2: Showing $\Psi$ Separates} To show $\Phi$ makes $X^+$ ad $X^-$ separable, we first need to show $\Psi$ does. For \cref{claim:bilx}(1), we first not that $\Psi$ is a valid output of \cref{alg:det_onelayer} on $X^+, X^-,$ and the chosen $\gamma$. Then, by \cref{thm:fin}, we can run \cref{alg:weights} to find vector $a\in \mathbb{R}^N$ such that the hyperplane $H(z):=a^{\intercal}z$ separates $\Psi(X^+)$ and $\Psi(X^-)$ with the margin at least $\sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$, i.e. \begin{equation} H(\Psi(x))=\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \relax(h_i(x)) =\begin{cases} \geq \Vert a\Vert \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N) &\textup{if }x\in X^+ \\ \leq - \Vert a\Vert\sqrt{N} \mathcal{M}(\gamma, N) &\textup{if }x\in X^- \end{cases}. \end{equation} For \cref{claim:bilx}(2), we first note that $\Psi$ is a valid output of \cref{alg:det_onelayer} on $C^+, C^-,$ and the chosen $\gamma$. By \cref{thm:arb}, $\Psi(X^+)$ and $\Psi(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin at least $\sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$. In fact, by the proof of \cref{thm:arb}, the separating hyperplane is of the form $H(z)=a^{\intercal}z$, i.e. \begin{equation} H(\Psi(x))=\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \relax(h_i(x)) =\begin{cases} \geq \Vert a\Vert \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N) &\textup{if }x\in X^+ \\ \leq - \Vert a\Vert\sqrt{N} \mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N) &\textup{if }x\in X^- \end{cases}. \end{equation} \paragraph{Step 3: Showing $\pi\circ\Phi$ Separates} Define real vector $\tilde{a}\in\mathbb{R}^\Sigma$ by \[\tilde{a}_j := \sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i \] for all $j\in \Sigma$. In words, $\tilde{a}_j$ is the sum of the weights $a_i$ over all $i$ where $h_i$ is a duplicate of $H_j$. Now, we show that the hyperplane $\tilde{H}(z):=\tilde{a}^{\intercal}z$ separates $\pi(\Phi(X^+))$ and $\pi(\Phi(X^-))$ with margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$. Note, for $j\in\Sigma$, $(\pi(\Phi(x)))_j = (\Phi(x))_j = \relax(H_j(x))$, and $H_j = h_i$ if $f(i)=j$. Hence \[ \tilde{H}(\pi(\Phi(x))) = \tilde{a}^{\intercal}\pi(\Phi(x)) = \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \tilde{a}_j(\pi(\Phi(x)))_{j} = \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \left(\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\right)\relax(H_j(x)) \] by the definition of $\tilde{a}_j$. Since $H_j=h_i$ if $f(i) = j$, we get \[ \tilde{H}(\pi(\Phi(x))) = \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\relax(h_i (x)) = \sum_{i=1}^Na_i\relax(h_i(x)) = H(\Psi(x)) \] by \eqref{eq:Hhci}. By \eqref{eq:Hhxi} and \eqref{eq:Hhci}, $(\pi\circ \Phi)(X^+)$ and $(\pi\circ \Phi)(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin at least $\Vert a\Vert \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)/\Vert \tilde{a}\Vert$ if $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite, and margin at least $\Vert a\Vert \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)/\Vert \tilde{a}\Vert$ otherwise. For each $j$, by Cauchy-Schwarz on each vector $(a_i)_i$ indexed by $i\in f^{-1}(j)\subset [N]$ \[ \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \tilde{a}_j^2 = \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \left(\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\right)^2 \leq \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \vert f^{-1}(j)\vert \sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i^2 \leq N \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i^2= N \sum_{i=1}^N a_i^2, \] where for a given $j$, $|f^{-1}(j)|$ is the number of indices $i$ such that $f(i) = j$. From this inequality, we get$\Vert \tilde{a}\Vert \leq \sqrt{N}\Vert a\Vert$. Thus, the separation margins are at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$ and $\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$, respectively. \paragraph{Step 4: Showing $\Phi$ Separates} By \cref{lem:proj}, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$ or $\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$, depending on if $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite. This proves \cref{claim:bilx}. \end{proof} To show \cref{thm:main,thm:main in k}, it suffices to bound the probability that for every $i$, $B_i^\ell(X)$ and $B_i^\ell(C)$ occurs for some $\ell$, as in the following claim. \begin{claim} For any $\delta$-separated sets $X^+, X^-\subset R\mathbb{B}_2^d$ with $N= \vert X^+\vert +\vert X^-\vert <\infty$, define $\Phi$ as in the three cases in \cref{thm:main,thm:main in k}, and define $B_i^\ell(X)$ as in \eqref{eq:bxil}. Then, $\mathbb{P}\left((\forall i)(\exists \ell)B_{i}^{\ell}(X)\right)\geq 1-\eta$ provided the width bounds on $n$ from \cref{thm:main,thm:main in k} are met in each case. \end{claim} \begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{claim:bil prob}] We break this proof down into two steps which we outline here. First, we will obtain bounds of $\mathbb{P}(B_i^\ell(X))$ similar to \cref{thm:prob}, except we include the case where no such $j$ exists as in \eqref{eq:bxil} and \eqref{eq:bcil}. Then, we use these bounds to obtain a final bound on $\mathbb{P}\left((\forall i)(\exists \ell)B_{i}^{\ell}(X)\right)$. \paragraph{Step 1: Bounding Each $\mathbb{P}(B_i^\ell(X))$} If $j$ exists in \eqref{eq:bxil}, \cref{thm:prob} gives bounds $p$, $p/10$, and $q$ of $\mathbb{P}(B_i^\ell(X))$ for any $i$ and $\ell$, depending on $\Phi$ as in \cref{thm:main,thm:main in k}. We show the same result for the easier case where no such $j$ exists by reducing it to \cref{thm:prob}. If no such $j$ exists \[ B^{\ell}_{i}(X) = \left\lbrace H_{\ell}(x_{i})\geq \gamma \right\rbrace \cap \lbrace\exists \ x\in R\mathbb{B}_2^d: H_\ell(x)\leq 0\rbrace. \] Since $\delta\leq 2R$, we can pick any $x_j\in R\mathbb{B}_2^d$ such that $\Vert x_j-x_i\Vert \geq \delta$. Then \[\mathbb{P}\left(\left\lbrace H_{\ell}(x_{i}) \geq \gamma \right\rbrace \cap \lbrace\exists \ x\in R\mathbb{B}_2^d: H_\ell(x)\leq 0\rbrace\right) \geq \mathbb{P}\left(\left\lbrace H_{\ell}(x_{i})\geq \gamma \right\rbrace \cap \lbrace H_\ell (x_j)\leq -\gamma\rbrace\right). \] If $\Vert x_i\Vert \geq \Vert x_j\Vert$, then this is precisely event $B_i$ in \cref{thm:prob} where we want the random hyperplane $H_\ell$ to separate $x_i$ from the singleton set $\lbrace x_j\rbrace$ with parameter $\gamma$. nodes.name: Notation and goal
nodes.statement: We modify the notation slightly for convenience of proving both finite set cases and arbitrary set cases together. Fix $\gamma$ to be either $\delta^2/8Rd$ or $\delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}$ depending on the distribution of $\Phi$, as in the finite set cases. For the arbitrary set cases, the parameter will be $\gamma/2$. We show in all three cases that provided the respective width bounds are met, with probability $1-\eta$, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are linearly separable. If $\vert X^+\vert +\vert X^-\vert = N <\infty$, then $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ will be linearly separable with margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$. Otherwise, in the case of arbitrary sets, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ will be linearly separable with margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$ where $N$ is now the $(\delta, 8R^2/\gamma)$-mutual complexity. We can check it is so for $\gamma\in\lbrace \delta^2/8Rd, \delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}\rbrace$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix γ and state the margins to prove

nodes.name: Points and signs
nodes.statement: For finite sets $X^+$ and $X^-$, recall $x_i$ and $\sigma$ from \cref{alg:det_onelayer} and \eqref{eq:sigma}. For arbitrary sets $X^+$ and $X^-$, let $C^{+}$ and $C^{-}$ be the finite sets of centers guaranteed by \cref{def:complexity} for $(\delta, 8R^2/\gamma)$-mutual complexity. Let $c_{i}$ be the point in $C^{+}\cup C^{-}$ with the $i$-th largest norm and let $\sigma : C^{+}\cup C^{-}\to \lbrace -1, +1\rbrace$ such that $\sigma (c)=+1$ if $c\in C^{+}$ and $\sigma (c)=-1$ if $c\in C^{-}$.

nodes.name: Events B_i^ℓ
nodes.statement: For a random layer $\Phi(x)=\relax (Wx+b)$ with width $n$, we let $B_i^j$ for $1\leq i\leq N$ and $1\leq \ell\leq n$ be the event that the $\ell$-th random hyperplane $H_\ell(z)=W_\ell^{\intercal}z+b_\ell$ of $\Phi$ satisfies the condition for $h_i$ in \cref{alg:det_onelayer} applied to $X^+$ and $X^-$ when they are finite or on $C^+$ and $C^-$ otherwise, and parameter $\gamma$. nodes.name: Claim 3.2 and its proof
nodes.statement: \begin{claim} Fix $\gamma$ to be $\delta^2/8Rd$ or $\delta^2/18R\sqrt{k}$. Recall $\mathcal{M}$ from \eqref{eq:p}. Then \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose that $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite and that for every $i$, $B_i^\ell(X)$ with parameter $\gamma$ holds for some $\ell$. Then, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$. \item For arbitrary sets $X^+$ and $X^-$, suppose that for every $i$, $B_i^\ell(C)$ with parameter $\gamma$ holds for some $\ell$. Then, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin $\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$. \end{enumerate} \end{claim} \begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{claim:bilx}] We break this proof down into four steps which we outline here. First, we set up some notation to clarify why we cannot directly apply \cref{alg:weights}. Then, we use \cref{thm:fin,thm:arb} to show that if we allow a single random hyperplane $H_\ell(z)$ to satisfy the condition for two hyperplanes $h_{i_1}$ and $h_{i_2}$, it makes the sets separable. Next, we show how to remove one of such hyperplanes while still making the sets separable. Finally, we use \cref{lem:proj} to show $\Phi$ also makes the sets separable. The margin will be tracked throughout. \paragraph{Step 1: Setup} By assumption, we can define indices map $f:[N]\to [n]$ by letting $f(i)=\ell$ if $B_i^\ell$ holds, where $B_i^\ell$ is either $B_i^\ell (X)$ or $B_i^\ell (C)$ depending on whether $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite. For a given $i$, if there are multiple $\ell$ such that $B_i^\ell$ holds, define $f(i)$ to be any such $\ell$. Define the range $\Sigma :=f([N])\subset [n]$ and let $\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^N$ be the projection onto the coordinates indexed by $\Sigma$. When $f$ is not injective, we cannot apply \cref{thm:fin} directly to $\lbrace H_j:j\in\Sigma\rbrace$ since there are less than $N$ hyperplanes. Let $h_i:=H_{f(i)}$ with another \emph{duplicated} hyperplane $h_{i'}$, i.e. $h_i$ and $h_{i'}$ are two copies of $H_j$ if $f(i)=f(i')=j$. Then, $h_i$ satisfies the condition on line 5 of \cref{alg:det_onelayer} for this $i$. Consider the one-layer neural network $\Psi(x)=\relax(h_1(x), \dots, h_N(x))$. \paragraph{Step 2: Showing $\Psi$ Separates} To show $\Phi$ makes $X^+$ ad $X^-$ separable, we first need to show $\Psi$ does. For \cref{claim:bilx}(1), we first not that $\Psi$ is a valid output of \cref{alg:det_onelayer} on $X^+, X^-,$ and the chosen $\gamma$. Then, by \cref{thm:fin}, we can run \cref{alg:weights} to find vector $a\in \mathbb{R}^N$ such that the hyperplane $H(z):=a^{\intercal}z$ separates $\Psi(X^+)$ and $\Psi(X^-)$ with the margin at least $\sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$, i.e. \begin{equation} H(\Psi(x))=\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \relax(h_i(x)) =\begin{cases} \geq \Vert a\Vert \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N) &\textup{if }x\in X^+ \\ \leq - \Vert a\Vert\sqrt{N} \mathcal{M}(\gamma, N) &\textup{if }x\in X^- \end{cases}. \end{equation} For \cref{claim:bilx}(2), we first note that $\Psi$ is a valid output of \cref{alg:det_onelayer} on $C^+, C^-,$ and the chosen $\gamma$. By \cref{thm:arb}, $\Psi(X^+)$ and $\Psi(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin at least $\sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$. In fact, by the proof of \cref{thm:arb}, the separating hyperplane is of the form $H(z)=a^{\intercal}z$, i.e. \begin{equation} H(\Psi(x))=\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \relax(h_i(x)) =\begin{cases} \geq \Vert a\Vert \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N) &\textup{if }x\in X^+ \\ \leq - \Vert a\Vert\sqrt{N} \mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N) &\textup{if }x\in X^- \end{cases}. \end{equation} \paragraph{Step 3: Showing $\pi\circ\Phi$ Separates} Define real vector $\tilde{a}\in\mathbb{R}^\Sigma$ by \[\tilde{a}_j := \sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i \] for all $j\in \Sigma$. In words, $\tilde{a}_j$ is the sum of the weights $a_i$ over all $i$ where $h_i$ is a duplicate of $H_j$. Now, we show that the hyperplane $\tilde{H}(z):=\tilde{a}^{\intercal}z$ separates $\pi(\Phi(X^+))$ and $\pi(\Phi(X^-))$ with margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$. Note, for $j\in\Sigma$, $(\pi(\Phi(x)))_j = (\Phi(x))_j = \relax(H_j(x))$, and $H_j = h_i$ if $f(i)=j$. Hence \[ \tilde{H}(\pi(\Phi(x))) = \tilde{a}^{\intercal}\pi(\Phi(x)) = \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \tilde{a}_j(\pi(\Phi(x)))_{j} = \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \left(\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\right)\relax(H_j(x)) \] by the definition of $\tilde{a}_j$. Since $H_j=h_i$ if $f(i) = j$, we get \[ \tilde{H}(\pi(\Phi(x))) = \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\relax(h_i (x)) = \sum_{i=1}^Na_i\relax(h_i(x)) = H(\Psi(x)) \] by \eqref{eq:Hhci}. By \eqref{eq:Hhxi} and \eqref{eq:Hhci}, $(\pi\circ \Phi)(X^+)$ and $(\pi\circ \Phi)(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin at least $\Vert a\Vert \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)/\Vert \tilde{a}\Vert$ if $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite, and margin at least $\Vert a\Vert \sqrt{N}\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)/\Vert \tilde{a}\Vert$ otherwise. For each $j$, by Cauchy-Schwarz on each vector $(a_i)_i$ indexed by $i\in f^{-1}(j)\subset [N]$ \[ \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \tilde{a}_j^2 = \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \left(\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\right)^2 \leq \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \vert f^{-1}(j)\vert \sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i^2 \leq N \sum_{j\in\Sigma} \sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i^2= N \sum_{i=1}^N a_i^2, \] where for a given $j$, $|f^{-1}(j)|$ is the number of indices $i$ such that $f(i) = j$. From this inequality, we get$\Vert \tilde{a}\Vert \leq \sqrt{N}\Vert a\Vert$. Thus, the separation margins are at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$ and $\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$, respectively. \paragraph{Step 4: Showing $\Phi$ Separates} By \cref{lem:proj}, $\Phi(X^+)$ and $\Phi(X^-)$ are linearly separable with margin at least $\mathcal{M}(\gamma, N)$ or $\mathcal{M}(\gamma/2, N)$, depending on if $X^+$ and $X^-$ are finite. This proves \cref{claim:bilx}. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Claim 3.3 and its proof

The cases for \cref{thm:main}(ii) and \cref{thm:main in k} follow by replacing $p$ with $p/10$ and $q$, respectively. For convenience, let $\overline{B}$ be the complement of $B$. By a union bound over $i$ and independence of $\ell\in [n]$ \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}\left((\forall i)(\exists \ell)B_{i}^{\ell}(X)\right) & = 1-\mathbb{P}\left((\exists i)(\forall \ell)\overline{B_{i}^{\ell}(X)}\right) \\ & \ge 1-N\mathbb{P}\left((\forall \ell)\overline{B_{i}^{\ell}(X)}\right) \\ & \ge 1-N(1-p)^{n} \\ & \ge 1-\eta \end{align*} where we check $1-x\leq e^{-x}\ \forall \ x\in [0, 1]$, so the last inequality follows $(1-p)^n\leq \exp(-pn)\leq \eta/N$ by our bound on $n$. nodes.name: Combine claims
nodes.statement: Finally, \cref{claim:bilx} and \cref{claim:bil prob} together implies the finite set cases of \cref{thm:main,thm:main in k}. For the arbitrary set cases, apply \cref{claim:bil prob} to the $\delta$-separated finite sets $C^+, C^-\subset R\mathbb{B}_2^d$ to get that $\mathbb{P}\left((\forall i)(\exists \ell)B_{i}^{\ell}(C)\right)\geq 1-\eta$ provided the width bounds on $n$ in \cref{thm:main,thm:main in k} are met.
